answerCheck.reason: Interpret the independent random boundary points in the ordinary uniform arclength model. Each side has probability 1/4; vertices have measure zero. Given the first side, the second is the same, adjacent or opposite with probabilities 1/4, 1/2, 1/4. For a same-side ordered pair (u, v) in the unit parameter square, |u-v|>=1/2 gives two corner triangles of legs 1/2 and total area 1/4. For adjacent sides, let u, v be distances from their shared corner; distance below 1/2 is the quarter disk u^2+v^2<1/4, of area pi/16. On opposite sides the distance is at least 1, so success is certain. Total probability is (1/4)*(1/4)+(1/2)*(1-pi/16)+1/4=(26-pi)/32, yielding 26+1+32=59. Alternatively keep all 16 ordered side-pair parameter squares as disjoint equal-area pieces: the four same-side squares contribute total favorable area 1, the eight adjacent squares contribute 8-pi/2, and the four opposite squares contribute 4, out of total 16. This gives the same ratio directly, without requiring conditional-probability mastery. Equality-distance boundaries have area zero.

answerCheck.reason: The actual predicates for a truth-teller are (true,false,false), so the answers are YNN. A liar faces(false,false,true) and negates each, giving YYN. For an alternater the predicates are (false,true,false); starting with truth gives NNN, while starting with a lie gives YYY. Therefore only truth-tellers contribute to the difference between the first two yes counts:22-15=7. Each truth-teller receives exactly one candy, so A. All three totals are feasible:7 truth-tellers,6 liars,9 YYY alternaters and 9 NNN alternaters give31 children and yes counts 22,15,9. One method subtracts the count equations T+L+Y=22 and L+Y=15. An optional written calculation subtracts22-15 by borrowing one ten, giving 7; written subtraction is a method choice, not universal evidence of algorithm proficiency.

answerCheck.reason: The actual SVG has the stated pentagon ordering A, B, C, D, E, with AB the lower-left cut of the rectangle. For P=(x, y), the dot product (A-P)dot(B-P)=x(x-4)+y(y-2) is negative exactly when(x-2)^2+(y-1)^2<5. Thus the obtuse locus is the interior of the circle with diameter AB, center(2, 1), radius sqrt(5). There is also a purely angle-based locus argument: the diameter theorem gives a right angle at each other circle point Q. If angle BAP>=90 degrees, angle APB cannot be obtuse. Otherwise ray AP meets the circle again at Q. If P lies before Q, angle APB is the exterior angle of PBQ and exceeds the right angle at Q;if P is beyond Q, triangle PQB has its right angle at Q and angle APB is acute. This proves the same inside-circle criterion without dot products. The pentagon is the rectangle 0<=x<=2 pi+1, 0<=y<=4 cut by x+2 y>=4. The diameter AB lies on the cut line, and the circle is centered on that line, so the favorable part is its upper/right semicircle. This semicircle really fits: if x<=0 and x+2 y>=4, then y>=2-x/2 and squared center distance is at least(x-2)^2+(1-x/2)^2=5-5 x+5 x^2/4>=5;similarly y<=0 would give x>=4-2 y and squared distance at least 5(1-y)^2>=5. Its remaining extents satisfy y<=1+sqrt(5)<4 and x<=2+sqrt(5)<5<2 pi+1. Hence no additional clipping occurs. Favorable area is 5 pi/2. The pentagon area is 4*(2 pi+1)-(1/2)*4*2=8 pi, so the ratio is 5/16. Boundaries have area zero.

For a specified coordinate x to exceed twice both others, the region is 0<x<1, 0<=y<x/2, 0<=z<x/2. It is the pyramid with apex (0,0,0) and square base {x=1,0<=y,z<=1/2}, so its volume is (1/3)*1*(1/4)=1/12. The analogous y-largest and z-largest events are disjoint: two distinct nonnegative coordinates cannot each exceed twice the other. Their union is precisely the requested event. Add the three pyramid volumes to obtain 3/12=1/4, E. All boundaries have zero volume under the explicitly supplied continuous model.

answerCheck.reason: The original denominator excludes all its real roots, even when a numerator factor cancels. In a nonpositive set [a,b] union (c,d), a<b<c<d, the closed endpoints a,b must be numerator zeros not excluded by the denominator, and the open endpoints c,d must be denominator zeros. All four endpoints belong to {1,2,3,4,5}. Monicity and degree3 then leave one extra factor in each polynomial. To preserve the required signs and endpoint types, these factors must be the same (x-t): otherwise one gains an extra sign boundary or isolated zero, or changes a prescribed endpoint type. Write P=(x-a)(x-b)(x-t), Q=(x-c)(x-d)(x-t). The choices t=c and t=d are always valid, and define exactly the same function on exactly the same natural domain R minus {c,d}; they must not be counted twice as functions. A third possibility is the unused fifth integer e, but only if its removable hole lies outside the required nonpositive set. This happens for unused e=1,3,5, and fails for e=2 or4 because that hole would cut one of the required intervals. There are five ordered endpoint quadruples, giving five base functions, plus three distinct additional-domain-hole functions, hence eight distinct natural-domain functions. If removable holes are entirely disregarded in function identity, the count instead becomes five; that convention also gives no listed option. The source13 counts polynomial-pair representations: two for each of the five endpoint quadruples plus the three allowable unused-root representations. For a concrete duplicate, (P,Q)=((x-1)(x-2)(x-3),(x-3)^2(x-4)) and ((x-1)(x-2)(x-4),(x-3)(x-4)^2) both define (x-1)(x-2)/((x-3)(x-4)) on R minus {3,4}, with nonpositive set [1,2] union (3,4). The exact certificate independently enumerates all35*35=1225 monic cubic pairs from root multisets, evaluates every real sign cell and root-domain point using rational arithmetic, and confirms13 eligible pairs,8 natural-domain function classes and5 reduced expressions. None of the listed choices is the function count under either stated convention.

answerCheck.reason: The initial worlds are ordered distinct draws(a,b) with1<=a,b<=40. Alice cannot know who is larger exactly when2<=a<=39; a=1 would force Bob larger and a=40 would force Alice larger. After that public announcement, Bob knows the comparison only for b in{1,2,39,40}: with b=1 or 2 every remaining possible Alice value is larger, and with b=39 or 40 every possible Alice value is smaller; each b from 3 through 38 leaves both orders possible. Bob then truthfully announces primality, forcing b=2. Alice has a in{3,...,39}, and 100b+a lies between203 and 239. The only square there is 225, so a=25 and a+b=27, A. Every knowledge claim is checked over the current observation class after the previous announcement, not against the original world set.

answerCheck.reason: Bela opens at n/2. After each of his turns maintain symmetry of the previously chosen finite set under x->n-x. If Jenn legally chooses x, then for every old z its mirror n-z was also old, so |(n-x)-z|=|x-(n-z)|>1. The reply n-x is in [0,n]; it also avoids the new x because |x-n/2|>1 gives |x-(n-x)|>2. Thus every Jenn move has a legal Bela reply restoring symmetry. Termination is proved separately: if k sorted chosen points have consecutive gaps greater than 1, their total span exceeds k-1 but is at most n, so k<=n. Hence play is finite and Jenn is the first unable to move. Bela always wins, A, for every stated integer n>4. This is a direct verified construction, not a finite-subtraction-game classification.

answerCheck.reason: The expression equals u-3u² = 1/12 - 3(u-1/6)², so it is at most 1/12. Equality requires 2^t = 6t. The continuous function 2^t-6t is 1 at t=0 and -4 at t=1, so equality occurs for some t in (0,1). Alternatively, when 0<u<1/3, the factors 3u and 1-3u have sum 1 and product at most 1/4; outside that interval the expression is nonpositive.

answerCheck.reason: Under the ordinary uniform-interval interpretation, put t=min(x,1-x). Sine symmetry, monotonicity on [0,pi/2] and the unit-circle identity give the favorable y interval 1/2-t<y<1/2+t, of length 2*t. Plane areas yield P(a)=a for 0<a<=1/2 and P(a)=2-a-1/(2*a) for 1/2<=a<=1. At a=0, x=0 and the strict event is impossible, so P(0)=0 without dividing by a zero-area rectangle. AM-GM gives a+1/(2*a)>=sqrt(2); equivalently 2-sqrt(2)-P(a)=(a-1/sqrt(2))^2/a. Equality at a=1/sqrt(2) gives 2-sqrt(2), B, above the first-piece maximum 1/2. Preserve both optional optimization routes and the explicit uniform and degenerate-interval qualifications. No trigonometric derivative or unrestricted numerical-identity target is needed.

answerCheck.reason: Set F(theta)=1-3*sin(theta)+5*cos(3*theta), a continuous function. At theta=k*pi/3 for k=0,...,6, the cosine term is 5*(-1)^k and the remaining term lies in [-2,4]. Thus the signs alternate strictly: positive at even k and negative at odd k. The six successive open subintervals contain at least six distinct roots. For completeness put z=cos(theta)+i*sin(theta), so |z|=1 and z is nonzero. Integer polar powers give sin(theta)=(z-z^(-1))/(2i) and cos(3theta)=(z^3+z^(-3))/2. Multiplying the equation by 2*z^3 yields5*z^6+3*i*z^4+2*z^3-3*i*z^2+5=0. This nonzero degree-six polynomial has at most six distinct complex zeros: repeatedly factor z-a for each distinct zero, using the factor theorem and induction, so more than six distinct factors would exceed the degree. The map theta->z is one-to-one on(0,2*pi], and its endpoint z=1 is not a zero. Hence there are exactly six solutions, D. This upper-bound proof does not use the fundamental theorem of algebra or assert that every polynomial has a root.

answerCheck.reason: For x>0, taking logarithms gives F(x)=ln(x)-C*2^x=0, where C=ln(sqrt(2))/2^(sqrt(2))>0. There are no roots at x<=1. One root is a=sqrt(2). Also F(2)=ln(2)*(1-2/2^(sqrt(2)))>0 because sqrt(2)>1, and F(4)=ln(2)*(2-8/2^(sqrt(2)))<0 because sqrt(2)<2. Continuity gives another root beta in (2,4). To prove that these are all roots without unrepresented logarithmic/exponential derivative rules, take distinct u,v>0. AM-GM gives (u+v)/2>sqrt(u*v), hence ln((u+v)/2)>(ln(u)+ln(v))/2; applying AM-GM to 2^u,2^v gives 2^((u+v)/2)<(2^u+2^v)/2. Consequently F((u+v)/2)>(F(u)+F(v))/2. Repeated bisection proves the non-strict chord inequality at every dyadic weight by induction; continuity extends it to every real weight in [0,1]. If three zeros u<b<v existed, the midpoint m=(u+v)/2 would satisfy F(m)>0. Express b as a convex combination of m and the nearer endpoint u or v; its positive coefficient of F(m), together with the chord inequality, forces F(b)>0, a contradiction. Thus exactly the roots sqrt(2),beta occur. Their sum lies in (2+sqrt(2),4+sqrt(2)), a subset of [2,6), so D.

answerCheck.reason: The first duration is below 1, so Amelia always takes a second step. She stops after two exactly when t1+t2>1, an upper triangle of probability 1/2 in the unit square. Otherwise she takes the third step, even if the accumulated time still does not exceed1, because three is the stated maximum. The durations are independent of all increments, so the stopping count is independent of the displacement increments. Two increments exceed1 with probability 1/2. For three increments, the failure set x1+x2+x3<=1 is a tetrahedron in the unit cube, with base area 1/2 and height1, hence volume 1/6; success probability is 5/6. Total probability gives (1/2)(1/2)+(1/2)(5/6)=2/3, C. All equality boundaries have zero measure under the explicit independent continuous uniform model.

answerCheck.reason: Let p_n be the probability that all three occupancies have the same parity. Then p_0=1 and p_(n+1)=(1−p_n)/3, since from a mixed parity state only choosing the exceptional bin makes all parities agree. Thus p_n=1/4+(3/4)(−1/3)^n. For odd n=2023 this is the all-odd event, with probability (1−3^(−2022))/4, closest to 1/4.

answerCheck.derivedAnswer: E. 2 arcsin(1/4)/π, under independent uniform planar directions
answerCheck.reason: Under the ordinary independent uniform planar-direction model, condition on the first direction. Let phi in [0,pi] be the smaller deviation of the second direction from exact reversal. The two length-2 jumps form an isosceles displacement triangle; bisection gives final distance4*sin(phi/2). Since sine is increasing on[0,pi/2], distance<1 is equivalent to phi<2*arcsin(1/4), with the principal inverse sine in (0,pi/2). The favorable second directions form an arc of total angular measure4*arcsin(1/4) out of 2*pi. Thus probability=2*arcsin(1/4)/pi, E. The stem does not explicitly specify the joint direction distribution: for example, uniform first direction followed deterministically by its reversal gives probability 1, while a deterministic90-degree turn gives 0, and both constructions have uniform marginal directions. Preserve this modeling limitation separately; the displayed E is correct under the ordinary independent uniform planar interpretation.

answerCheck.reason: The frustum has radii3 and 6 and height3*sqrt(3), so its slant height is 6. Extend the cone: similar axial triangles give inner and outer developed radii6 and 12. Cone unfolding gives a sector of angle pi because the outer circular rim has circumference12*pi; diametrically opposite generators therefore differ by pi/2 in the developed angle. The straight developed chord enters the removed radius-6 disk and is inadmissible. Here is a global lower bound without assuming a new shortest-path theorem. Any continuous surface path lifts to the annular cone development with endpoint angular difference pi/2+k*pi for an integer k; after reflection its absolute angular difference is at least pi/2. It must cross the ray at angle pi/3 from A=(12,0). At a first such point P=(r/2,sqrt(3)*r/2), r>=6, the coordinate-distance formula gives AP^2=(r-6)^2+108>=108. Thus the path before P has length at least6*sqrt(3). The remaining path has net angular travel at least pi/6 and stays outside the radius-6 disk. Radial projection to that circle cannot increase length: for unit vectors u,v and r,s>=6, the squared distance identity |r*u-s*v|^2=(r-s)^2+r*s*|u-v|^2>=36*|u-v|^2 proves contraction for every chord. Apply it to every ordered path partition and take the supremum defining curve length; the projected path must cover circular angular travel at least pi/6, of length at least pi by the arc formula. Hence every path has length at least6*sqrt(3)+pi, including paths that wind or cross a development seam. Attainment is a tangent segment from A to the inner circle at angle pi/3, length 6*sqrt(3), followed by the inner-rim arc of angle pi/6, length pi. It stays within the annulus. Therefore the shortest length is 6*sqrt(3)+pi, E.
